questions.text: Which of the following transport mechanisms provides the primary driving force for the reabsorption of almost all solutes and water in the renal tubule?

options.A: Basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase generating low intracellular Na+ and a negative membrane potential
options.B: Apical pinocytosis of albumin and low molecular weight globulins
options.C: Transcellular simple passive diffusion of sodium across lipid bilayers
options.D: Direct vesicular exocytosis of intact filtrate across tubular cells
options.E: Paracellular solvent drag driven solely by medullary interstitial urea

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: In the Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT), what percentage of the filtered load of sodium, water, and potassium is normally reabsorbed?

options.A: Approximately 65% to 70% (isotonically reabsorbed)
options.C: Exactly 100% with no sodium reaching the loop of Henle
options.D: Less than 25% under normal resting conditions
options.E: 90% in cortical nephrons and 0% in juxtamedullary nephrons

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Why does the tubular fluid remaining at the end of the Proximal Convoluted Tubule remain strictly ISOSMOTIC (-290-300 mOsm/kg) to plasma?

options.A: The PCT reabsorbs sodium and solutes without any accompanying water
options.B: The PCT is completely impermeable to water along its entire length
options.C: Urea is actively pumped out of tubular cells into the lumen
options.D: Active water secretion balances active sodium reabsorption
options.E: Water is reabsorbed proportionally with solutes via Aquaporin-1

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Glomerulotubular (G-T) Balance is an intrinsic autoregulatory mechanism of the proximal tubule that ensures:

options.A: A constant absolute milligram amount of sodium is reabsorbed regardless of GFR
options.B: A constant percentage (~65-70%) of filtered load is reabsorbed despite GFR changes
options.C: The GFR is completely suppressed whenever blood pressure rises
options.D: Renal blood flow remains completely constant between 50 and 80 mmHg
options.E: The macula densa completely stops secreting adenosine during exercise

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Which peritubular capillary Starling force primarily drives the uptake of reabsorbed fluid from the proximal tubule interstitium back into the blood?

options.A: High peritubular capillary hydrostatic pressure (averaging -55 mmHg)
options.B: High peritubular interstitial oncotic pressure derived from lymphatics
options.C: Low interstitial hydrostatic pressure combined with zero oncotic pressure
options.D: Active pinocytosis by peritubular endothelial fenestrations
options.E: High peritubular capillary oncotic pressure (~32-35 mmHg) and low hydrostatic pressure (~13 mmHg)

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: During extracellular fluid volume expansion (e.g., rapid saline infusion), what happens to peritubular Starling forces and proximal tubular reabsorption?

options.A: Peritubular oncotic pressure rises steeply, accelerating fluid uptake
options.B: Proximal sodium reabsorption increases to 100%, causing total anuria
options.C: Peritubular oncotic falls and hydrostatic rises, inhibiting reabsorption
options.D: Peritubular capillary resistance increases 10-fold, stopping all blood flow
options.E: Glomerular ultrafiltration coefficient drops to zero immediately

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: The sodium-hydrogen antiporter NHE3 on the apical brush border membrane of the proximal tubule functions via:

options.A: Primary active transport requiring direct ATP hydrolysis by the carrier
options.B: Paracellular solvent drag driven by transcellular chloride reabsorption
options.C: Facilitated diffusion of protons into cells down an electrical gradient
options.D: Secondary active countertransport coupling Na+ influx with H+ efflux
options.E: Simple passive diffusion independent of sodium concentration gradients

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Approximately 85% to 90% of filtered bicarbonate (HCO3-) is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. This process is initiated apically by:

options.A: Direct apical uptake of filtered bicarbonate by an electrogenic symporter
options.B: Endocytosis of bicarbonate ions via clathrin-coated pits
options.C: Apical H+ secretion via NHE3, converting luminal HCO3- to H2CO3
options.D: Direct paracellular HCO3- diffusion driven by lumen-positive potential
options.E: Hydrolysis of bicarbonate into ammonium ions by glutaminase enzymes

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: The membrane-bound enzyme Carbonic Anhydrase IV (CA-IV) localized on the brush border of proximal

options.A: Synthesis of aldosterone from intracellular cholesterol precursors
options.B: Active transport of calcium ions across tight junctions
options.C: Rapid conversion of intracellular CO2 and H20 into carbonic acid
options.D: Hydrolysis of ATP to drive the basolateral sodium-potassium pump
options.E: Rapid dehydration of luminal H2CO3 into CO2 and H20 for passive

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Once inside the proximal tubule epithelial cell, bicarbonate is extruded across the basolateral membrane into the interstitial fluid primarily via:

options.A: Simple non-ionic passive diffusion across the lipid bilayer
options.B: The basolateral Na+-3HCO3- cotransporter (NBCe1 / electrogenic symport)
options.C: The apical NHE3 antiporter operating in a reverse direction
options.D: Apical CFTR chloride channels operating as bicarbonate exchangers
options.E: Direct vesicular exocytosis into the lumen of peritubular capillaries

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: In the early proximal tubule (S1 segment), glucose, amino acids, and phosphate are reabsorbed preferentially with sodium, resulting in:

options.A: A steep fall in luminal chloride concentration to near zero
options.B: A progressive increase in luminal chloride concentration (TF/P_CI > 1.0) along the tubule
options.C: Complete alkalinization of the tubular fluid to pH 9.0
options.D: Immediate precipitation of calcium oxalate crystals in all healthy nephrons
options.E: A massive drop in tubular fluid osmolality to 50 mOsm/kg

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: In the late proximal tubule (S2 and S3 segments), why does chloride reabsorption across tight junctions generate a slight lumen-positive potential (+2 to +4 mV)?

options.A: High active secretion of sodium ions into the tubular lumen
options.B: Direct binding of chloride to Tamm-Horsfall glycoprotein
options.C: Complete absence of basolateral sodium-potassium ATPase pumps
options.D: Rapid active secretion of potassium through apical ROMK channels
options.E: Chloride diffusion down its concentration gradient through anion-selective claudins

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: The lumen-positive potential (+2 to +4 mV) in the late proximal tubule is physiologically important because it drives the paracellular reabsorption of:

options.A: Glucose and neutral amino acids down their chemical gradients
options.B: Urea and uric acid via secondary active symport
options.C: Cations, including Na+, Ca2+, and Mg2+, across tight junctions
options.D: Bicarbonate ions against their electrical gradient
options.E: Tamm-Horsfall mucoproteins into the systemic circulation

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Filtered low-molecular-weight proteins and small peptide hormones (e.g., insulin, beta-2 microglobulin) are reabsorbed in the proximal tubule via:

options.A: Receptor-mediated endocytosis via Megalin-Cubilin complexes on apical membranes
options.B: Facilitated diffusion mediated by GLUT2 hexose transporters
options.C: Simple passive diffusion through tight junction aqueous pores
options.D: Paracellular solvent drag across claudin-2 water channels
options.E: Primary active transport coupled directly to apical H+ ATPase

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Question 15 covering high-yield concepts in Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture.

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: The high-capacity, low-affinity Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter SGLT2 is located on the apical membrane of which nephron segment?

options.A: Thick ascending limb of Henle in the outer medulla
options.B: Medullary collecting duct responding to antidiuretic hormone
options.C: Late distal convoluted tubule and initial connecting tubule
options.D: Early proximal tubule (S1 and S2 segments), reabsorbing ~90% of filtered glucose
options.E: Descending thin limb of Henle in juxtamedullary nephrons

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Once transported across the apical membrane by SGLT2, glucose exits the proximal tubular cell into the interstitial space across the basolateral membrane via:

options.A: Facilitated diffusion mediated by GLUT2 uniporters
options.B: Primary active transport by the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase
options.C: Paracellular retrograde back-leak through tight junctions
options.D: Apical countertransport coupled to hydrogen ion secretion
options.E: Receptor-mediated endocytosis into peritubular capillaries

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: In the late proximal tubule (S3 segment), the remaining ~10% of filtered glucose is cleared with high affinity and low capacity by:

options.A: SGLT1 cotransporters coupling 2 Na+ ions to 1 glucose molecule (exiting via basolateral GLUT1)
options.B: Simple non-ionic diffusion through paracellular pores
options.C: SGLT2 cotransporters coupling 1 Na+ to 1 glucose molecule
options.D: Apical NHE3 antiporters operating in reverse
options.E: Active pinocytosis followed by lysosomal degradation

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: In a healthy adult male, the maximum rate at which the kidneys can reabsorb glucose (Transport Maximum, Tm_G) averages approximately:

options.A: 50 mg/min
options.B: 375 mg/min (and -300 mg/min in healthy adult females)
options.C: 1000 mg/min
options.D: 125 mg/min (exactly equal to normal GFR
options.E: Infinite (glucose transport can never be saturated at any plasma level)

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Although theoretical Tm_G is reached at plasma glucose -300 mg/dL, glucose first appears in urine at a Renal Threshold' of ~180-200 mg/dL. This difference is known as:

options.A: The 'Splay' phenomenon (due to nephron heterogeneity and low carrier affinity near saturation)
options.B: The Bayliss myogenic reflex
options.C: Autoregulation of renal blood flow
options.D: The Filtration Fraction equilibrium
options.E: Glomerulotubular balance

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., Empagliflozin, Dapagliflozin) lower blood glucose in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus primarily by:

options.A: Directly stimulating insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells
options.B: Inhibiting apical SGLT2 in S1 PCT, inducing therapeutic glucosuria and natriuresis
options.C: Destroying GLUT2 transporters on hepatic cell membranes
options.D: Blocking glucose filtration across the glomerular basement membrane
options.E: Stimulating glucose synthesis by medullary collecting duct cells

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: The Organic Anion Transport (OAT) system in the proximal tubule actively secretes endogenous and exogenous anions, including:

options.A: Para-aminohippurate (PAH), penicillin, furosemide, thiazides, and urate
options.B: Sodium, chloride, and potassium ions
options.C: Glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate ions
options.D: Creatinine, morphine, and cimetidine only
options.E: Urea, inulin, and mannitol exclusively

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Basolateral uptake of organic anions (e.g., PAH, penicillin) into proximal tubule cells via OAT1 and OAT3 is an example of:

options.A: Simple passive diffusion driven by blood hydrostatic pressure
options.B: Direct primary ATP hydrolysis by the OAT transporter protein
options.C: Paracellular bulk flow across claudin-1 tight junctions
options.D: Tertiary active transport (coupled to outward movement of alpha-ketoglutarate down its gradient)
options.E: Receptor-mediated endocytosis via clathrin-coated pits

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Why does co-administration of Probenecid prolong the half-life and therapeutic blood levels of Penicillin?

options.A: Probenecid destroys bacterial beta-lactamase enzymes directly
options.B: Probenecid precipitates penicillin into insoluble crystals in muscle
options.C: Probenecid competitively inhibits basolateral OAT transporters, blocking tubular secretion of penicillin
options.D: Probenecid stimulates hepatic metabolism of all beta-lactam antibiotics
options.E: Probenecid blocks glomerular filtration of penicillin across the GBM

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: The Organic Cation Transport (OCT) system secretes cationic drugs (e.g., cimetidine). Apical exit via MATE is driven by:

options.A: Simple non-ionic passive diffusion down electrical gradients
options.B: Direct ATP hydrolysis by basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase
options.C: Paracellular solvent drag across anion-selective pores
options.D: Binding to filtered Tamm-Horsfall glycoprotein in the lumen
options.E: Electroneutral H+/organic cation antiport driven by lumen H+ gradient

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Uric acid handling in the human kidney is complex and involves which sequential four-component process in the proximal tubule?

options.A: Non-filtration, complete distal secretion, and collecting duct uptake
options.B: Complete filtration with zero reabsorption (clearance equals GFR)
options.C: Primary active secretion in the thin ascending limb without any filtration
options.D: Filtration, reabsorption (via URAT1), secretion, and post-secretory uptake
options.E: Continuous synthesis by tubular epithelial cells from urea precursors

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: The uricosuric drug Probenecid promotes urinary excretion of uric acid in patients with chronic gout primarily by:

options.A: Inhibiting apical URAT1 and GLUT9, blocking proximal urate reabsorption
options.B: Stimulating filtration of uric acid by dilating afferent arterioles
options.C: Inhibiting xanthine oxidase in hepatocytes, blocking uric acid synthesis
options.D: Binding uric acid in the bladder to form soluble calcium salts
options.E: Acidifying the urine to convert uric acid into volatile ammonia gas

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Hartnup Disease is an inherited renal and intestinal transport defect involving the BOAT1 transporter, resulting in defective tubular reabsorption of:

options.A: Dicarboxylic amino acids (glutamate and aspartate) causing renal calculi
options.B: Basic amino acids (cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine / COLA)
options.C: Inorganic phosphate, leading to isolated X-linked hypophosphatemia
options.D: Neutral amino acids (especially Tryptophan), predisposing to Pellagra-like symptoms (dementia, dermatitis, diarrhea)
options.E: Glucose and galactose, leading to severe neonatal lactic acidosis

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Cystinuria is caused by defective apical reabsorption of dibasic amino acids via the rBAT/b0,+AT transporter, clinically causing renal stones composed of:

options.A: Cholesterol plaques originating from the renal capsule
options.B: Coffin-lid shaped Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) crystals
options.C: Needle-shaped uric acid crystals soluble only in strong acid
options.D: Pure calcium phosphate crystals resulting from distal RTA
options.E: Hexagonal, radiopaque Cystine crystals (due to poor solubility of cystine at acidic urine pH)

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: The Thick Ascending Limb of Henle (TAL) reabsorbs ~25% of filtered NaCl via the apical NKCC2 cotransporter. This carrier is classified as:

options.A: Primary active electrogenic pump powered directly by ATP hydrolysis
options.B: Uniporter facilitating passive potassium entry down chemical gradients
options.C: Passive paracellular channel gated by extracellular calcium levels
options.D: Secondary active electroneutral symporter transporting 1 Na+, 1 K+, and 2 Cl- ions into the cell
options.E: Tertiary countertransporter coupled to bicarbonate exit into the lumen

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Bartter Syndrome is an autosomal recessive tubulopathy caused by inactivating mutations in TAL transport proteins (NKCC2, ROMK, or CIC-Kb), mimicking chronic use of:

options.A: Thiazide diuretics (inhibiting distal convoluted tubule NCC)
options.B: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (inhibiting proximal bicarbonate uptake)
options.C: Osmotic diuretics (e.g., Mannitol), causing massive hypernatremia
options.D: Potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g., Amiloride), causing severe hyperkalemia
options.E: Loop diuretics (e.g., Furosemide), presenting with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hypercalciuria, and normal BP

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: In the early Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT), ~5% of filtered NaCl is reabsorbed across the apical membrane via:

options.A: The amiloride-sensitive epithelial sodium channel (ENaC)
options.B: The Sodium-Hydrogen antiporter NHE3 coupled to carbonic anhydrase
options.C: SGLT1 cotransporters operating without glucose
options.D: Paracellular solvent drag driven by medullary countercurrent gradients
options.E: The electroneutral Sodium-Chloride Cotransporter (NCC), which is inhibited by Thiazide Diuretics

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Gitelman Syndrome is an inherited loss-of-function tubulopathy of the thiazide-sensitive NCC cotransporter in the DCT, characteristically featuring:

options.A: Hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis with severe hypertension
options.B: Severe hypercalciuria with recurrent staghorn calculi
options.C: Hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, and HYPOCALCIURIA (reduced urinary calcium excretion)
options.D: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with cellular crescent formation
options.E: Profound generalized aminoaciduria and glucosuria (Fanconi phenotype)

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Question 36 covering high-yield concepts in Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture.

options.A: Primary renal physiological mechanism

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Liddle Syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by 'gain-of-function' mutations in ENaC subunits that prevent channel degradation, resulting in:

options.A: Salt wasting, hypotension, hyperkalemia, and high aldosterone levels
options.B: Massive proteinuria with generalized nephrotic edema
options.C: Hyperactivation of ENaC: severe hypertension, hypokalemia, low renin/aldo
options.D: Isolated renal glucosuria with perfectly normal blood pressure
options.E: Defective urinary concentration mimicking nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Aldosterone promotes sodium reabsorption and potassium/hydrogen secretion in the collecting duct by binding to intracellular mineralocorticoid receptors and:

options.A: Stimulating rapid degradation of medullary aquaporin-2 water channels
options.B: Increasing apical insertion of ENaC and basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase units
options.C: Directly inhibiting the basolateral sodium-potassium ATPase pump
options.D: Blocking all hydrogen ion secretion by Type A intercalated cells
options.E: Decreasing the activity of renal outer medullary potassium channels

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Type A Intercalated Cells of the collecting duct are primarily responsible for acid secretion and bicarbonate regeneration during acidosis via apical:

options.A: Carbonic anhydrase IV operating as a sodium cotransporter
options.B: SGLT2 cotransporters pumping bicarbonate against chemical gradients
options.C: Vacuolar H+-ATPase and H+/K+-ATPase pumps, extruding H+ into urine
options.D: Pendrin (anion exchanger) secreting bicarbonate into the tubular lumen
options.E: ENaC sodium channels operating in reverse to expel protons

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Type B Intercalated Cells function during systemic metabolic alkalosis to eliminate excess base. They accomplish this via apical expression of:

options.A: NHE3 antiporters pumping bicarbonate directly into the blood
options.B: Vacuolar H+-ATPase pumps facing the tubular lumen exclusively
options.C: ROMK channels coupled to basolateral Megalin receptors
options.D: Pendrin (apical CI-/HCO3- exchanger), which actively secretes bicarbonate into tubular fluid
options.E: Aquaporin-2 channels transporting liquid alkali into the urine

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH / Vasopressin) regulates water permeability in principal cells of the collecting duct by binding basolateral V2 receptors and:

options.A: Directly opening paracellular tight junctions to allow bulk water flow
options.B: Gs-adenylyl cyclase-cAMP signaling inserting Aquaporin-2 into apical membrane
options.C: Phosphorylating apical NKCC2 cotransporters to pump water into tissue
options.D: Blocking basolateral AQP3 and AQP4 channels, trapping water in cells
options.E: Activating Gq-phospholipase C to degrade intracellular aquaporin stores

questions.masterclass_title: Renal Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion - Physiology Lecture

questions.text: Osmotic Diuresis occurs when unreabsorbed, non-reabsorbable solutes remain in the tubular lumen (e.g., Mannitol, or Glucose exceeding Tm_G). The mechanism is:

options.A: Direct chemical destruction of the renal outer medullary collecting ducts
options.B: Retrograde filtration of urine from the pelvis back into glomerular capillaries
options.C: Inhibition of systemic antidiuretic hormone release by pituitary
options.D: Luminal osmotic pressure opposes water uptake, sweeping water into urine
options.E: Direct toxic stimulation of the adrenal cortex to hypersecrete aldosterone
